drivers.driver: The ongoing uncertainty surrounding a privatization process requires public intervention to ensure minority interests are protected from potential self-dealing [D01].
Operating results are showing signs of life with positive adjusted EBITDA, justifying a more proactive stance to unlock value [D03].
Super-voting control structures create a governance gap that necessitates public scrutiny to prevent value leakage [D01].

final.memo:
Soho House possesses a unique membership hospitality platform with durable demand, yet its corporate structure and governance currently obscure significant underlying value [D01]. While Q3 results demonstrate improved adjusted EBITDA of $48.3 million and solid membership growth, the path to sustained GAAP profitability and capital return remains tethered to a model burdened by expansionary capex and lease obligations [D03; D05].

Our primary concern is the potential privatization process, which must not occur in a vacuum [D01]. Given the influence of super-voting shares and the inherent conflict in any management-led transaction, we believe it is time to move from private monitoring to a more public escalation [D01]. Minority shareholders require transparent assurance that any future sale or restructuring process is governed by an independent committee and directed toward a competitive auction, rather than a controlled outcome that undervalues the franchise [D01; D05].

We have no interest in waiting for the market to resolve these governance questions on its own [D01]. By forcing a public discussion on board independence and fair-process requirements, we aim to protect our investment from the risk of empire-building or a distressed exit at an inadequate valuation [D05]. We maintain our position with the firm expectation that management and the board will adhere to the highest fiduciary standards as they navigate this inflection point [D01; D07].
